report_title: Cotton Sandstorm / Emennet Pasargad (Aria Sepehr Ayandehsazan, ASA) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: Primary sources: (1) Joint FBI / U.S. Department of the Treasury / Israel National Cyber Directorate (INCD) Cybersecurity Advisory 'New Tradecraft of Iranian Cyber Group Aria Sepehr Ayandehsazan aka Emennet Pasargad', Product ID AA24-233A / JCSA-20241030-001, 2024-10-30 (https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2024/241030.pdf), which maps this actor's TTPs and IOCs to MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise v15.1 and supersedes the 2022-10-20 FBI PIN (https://www.ic3.gov/Media/News/2022/221020.pdf). (2) Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 'As the U.S. election nears, Russia, Iran and China step up influence efforts' / 'Iran surges cyber-enabled influence operations in support of Hamas', which tracks this actor as Cotton Sandstorm and documents the 'For-Humanity' generative-AI IPTV operation, IP-camera harvesting, and 'Cyber Court' cover-hacktivist persona network (https://blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2024/10/23/as-the-u-s-election-nears-russia-iran-and-china-step-up-influence-efforts/). (3) Check Point Research WezRat analysis for the 'bd.exe' remote access trojan family. Every technique_id in the ttps array was verified to exist in this environment's bundled (reorganized) ATT&CK dataset via `sigma.data.mitre_attack.mitre_attack_techniques`; the defense-evasion tactic is emitted as 'stealth' per this dataset's convention. NOTE ON GROUP ID: the task brief asserts MITRE tracks Emennet Pasargad as G1009, but in this environment's bundled dataset G1009 resolves to 'Moses Staff' (an unrelated Iranian hack-and-leak/wiper group) and G1044 resolves to APT42 — there is NO Emennet Pasargad / Cotton Sandstorm group object in this dataset, so no G-ID base mapping was inheritable and the extraction is built directly from the advisory's own ATT&CK table plus enrichment. NO IOCs were taken from advisory AA24-290A (a separate Iranian brute-force credential-access actor whose IPs/hashes/CVE-2020-1472 are unrelated to Cotton Sandstorm).

actor.name: Cotton Sandstorm
related_clusters: IRGC — assessed sponsoring body; ASA operates as a nominal cover company (Iranian Registration Number 504415) providing HR/financial cover for IRGC-nexus operators

Moses Staff / DEV-0500 / Marigold Sandstorm (G1009 in this dataset) — a DISTINCT but ideologically-similar Iranian hack-and-leak/anti-Israel group; NOT the same actor as Cotton Sandstorm despite the task's G1009 reference. Included here only to flag the group-ID collision, not as an alias

Cover-hacktivist personas run BY ASA: 'Makhlab al-Nasr', 'NET Hunter', 'Emirate Students Movement', 'Zeus is Talking' (zeusistalking[.]io/net/com), 'Regiment GUD' (rgud-group[.]net/com; impersonates real French far-right group GUD), 'Anzu Team' (operation vs Sweden)
Lebanon-based hosting clients supported by ASA cover-resellers (alqassam[.]ps HAMAS military-wing site; almaq[.]org)
actor.attribution: Iranian state-sponsored cyber-enabled information-operations actor, assessed by FBI/Treasury/INCD and Microsoft to be affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Two Emennet Pasargad-linked Iranian nationals were previously indicted by the U.S. DOJ for the 2020 U.S. presidential-election voter-intimidation/disinformation campaign, and the U.S. Rewards for Justice program offers up to $10M for information on the group. Group attribution to Iran/IRGC is high-confidence and convergent across U.S. government, Israeli government, and Microsoft reporting. Per the advisory's own caveat, individual TTPs/IOCs can overlap with third-party actors who purchase access, so single-indicator attribution should be avoided.
targeted_regions_mena: United Arab Emirates (Emirate Students Movement persona targeting)
targeted_regions_global: United Kingdom (cover-reseller infrastructure via Stark Industries/PQ Hosting)
targeted_sectors: Sports / international events (2024 Paris Olympic & Paralympic Games)
Israeli military and defense personnel (fighter pilots, UAV operators)
Critical infrastructure and general Israeli commercial entities (hack-and-leak)

key_campaigns.name: 2020 U.S. Presidential election voter-intimidation & false-flag disinformation (Emennet Pasargad)
key_campaigns.summary: Original Emennet Pasargad hack-and-leak / cyber-enabled influence operation that sent intimidating emails to U.S. voters posing as the Proud Boys, produced a video alleging election-system vulnerabilities, and accessed election-related infrastructure — leading to a DOJ indictment of two Iranian nationals. Established the group's signature blend of intrusion plus exaggerated/fictitious claims to maximize psychological effect.

key_campaigns.name: Israel hack-and-leak operations (pre-2022 PIN baseline)
key_campaigns.summary: Hack-and-leak operations against primarily Israeli organizations, combining data theft with information operations that inflict financial loss and reputational damage, using false-flag personas and exaggerated claims of access. Documented in the 2022-10-20 FBI PIN that this advisory supersedes.

key_campaigns.name: Contact-HSTG / Cyber Flood hostage-family intimidation
key_campaigns.summary: Following the 7 October 2023 HAMAS attack, ASA used cover personas 'Cyber Flood' and 'Contact-HSTG' to send threatening SMS/messaging to family members of Israeli hostages (via https://Contact-hstg[.]com forms), posing as Al-Qassam to cause additional psychological trauma.

key_campaigns.name: For-Humanity IPTV compromise with generative-AI news anchor
key_campaigns.summary: Under the 'For-Humanity' persona, ASA leveraged unauthorized access to a US-based IPTV streaming company to disseminate crafted Israel-Hamas-war messaging, notably incorporating a generative-AI-generated fake news anchor. Part of a broader adoption of AI services (Remini AI Photo Enhancer, Voicemod, Murf AI voice modulation, Appy Pie image generation).

key_campaigns.name: IP-camera / RTSP surveillance harvesting
key_campaigns.summary: Hours after the Oct-7 attack, ASA enumerated internet-facing IP addresses running Real Time Streaming Protocol (TCP/554), primarily in Israel but also Gaza and Iran, and made harvested camera images/content available to clients via several servers (e.g. 5.230.56[.]148, 77.91.74[.]158; platform later at 195.26.87[.]80, 213.109.147[.]97, 185.110.188[.]112).

key_campaigns.name: Cyber Court cover-hacktivist promotion network
key_campaigns.summary: ASA operated the online persona 'Cyber Court' (cybercourt[.]io, Telegram @cybercourt_io) to amplify the activities of several ASA-run cover-hacktivist groups — Makhlab al-Nasr, NET Hunter, Emirate Students Movement, Zeus is Talking — as apparent grassroots protest of the Israel-Hamas conflict. Also developed a crowdsourced 'Sample' campaign to identify and intimidate Israeli law-enforcement individuals.

key_campaigns.name: 2024 Paris Olympics dynamic-display compromise (Regiment GUD false flag)
key_campaigns.summary: Using 'VPS-Agent' cover infrastructure, ASA compromised a French commercial dynamic-display provider to show photo montages denouncing Israeli athletes' participation in the 2024 Olympic/Paralympic Games, coupled with a fake news article on a spoofed French collaborative-media site and threat messages to Israeli athletes under the banner of a fake French far-right group 'Regiment GUD' (impersonating the real group GUD).

key_campaigns.name: Anzu Team operation against Sweden
key_campaigns.summary: Cyber-enabled information operation against Sweden conducted under the 'Anzu Team' banner, corroborated by public statements from the Swedish Security Service and Sweden's Prosecutor's Office.

malware: WezRat (aka 'bd' / bd.exe / First.exe) — heavily-obfuscated remote access trojan that collects basic host information and connects to a hard-coded web server for tasking; delivered via a trojanized 'Google Chrome Installer.msi' that runs the RAT after a legitimate Chrome install/update; uses a command-line de-obfuscation key (observed '8765') and C2 web-server 'connect.il-cert[.]net'; C2 paths http://onlinelive[.]info/wez/insert.php and /wez/api.php
tooling_observed: Masscan (IP-block / port scanning, incl. RTSP TCP/554 enumeration)
knowem[.]com, facecheck[.]id, socialcatfish[.]com, peekyou[.]com, ancestry[.]com, familysearch[.]org — people-search / reverse-image / username checks
Wikimapia[.]org, OpenStreetMap (openstreetmap.org), Pastebin, Instagram, LinkedIn — location/OSINT correlation
Commercial VPNs: Private Internet Access, Windscribe, ExpressVPN, Urban VPN, NordVPN

Fictitious cover-hosting resellers 'Server-Speed' (server-speed[.]com, ~Apr 2023–May 2024) and 'VPS-Agent' (vps-agent[.]net, ~May 2024 onward); upstream from BAcloud (Lithuania) and Stark Industries Solutions / PQ Hosting (UK/Moldova)
Generative-AI services: Remini AI Photo Enhancer, Voicemod (voicemod.net), Murf AI (murf.ai) voice modulation, Appy Pie image generation

Cover personas & channels: Cyber Court (cybercourt[.]io, Telegram @cybercourt_io), Cyber Flood, Contact-HSTG (Contact-hstg[.]com), For-Humanity, Regiment GUD (rgud-group[.]net/com), Zeus is Talking (zeusistalking[.]io/net/com), Anzu Team, Makhlab al-Nasr, NET Hunter, Emirate Students Movement

ttps.procedure_description: ASA uses open technical-database services to find internet-exposed targets: Shodan (shodan[.]io) to identify infrastructure hosting IP cameras and other devices, and ip2location[.]com for network geolocation, when conducting reconnaissance and enumeration against organizations.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — third-party database queries occur entirely off-victim and leave no defender-side telemetry; a HUNT/attack-surface-awareness item (know what of yours is indexed in Shodan) rather than a log detection

ttps.procedure_description: When targeting individuals, ASA profiles identities using people-search, reverse-image and username-check services — knowem[.]com, facecheck[.]id, ancestry[.]com, socialcatfish[.]com, peekyou[.]com, familysearch[.]org — to build dossiers on targets such as Israeli fighter pilots and UAV operators.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim OSINT against public/commercial data sources; not observable in defender telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses
ttps.procedure_description: ASA harvests target email addresses associated with particular domains using services such as snov[.]io, email-format[.]com and hunter[.]io to seed messaging, phishing and account-targeting.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — email-address enumeration is off-victim; a threat-intel/hunt awareness item

ttps.technique_name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Employee Names
ttps.procedure_description: ASA researches potential victims and their roles on social media including Instagram and LinkedIn, and used a Python script to correlate Instagram location data with OpenStreetMap to identify individuals of interest (e.g. Israeli military personnel).
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — social-media reconnaissance is off-victim; not detectable in enterprise telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Gather Victim Org Information: Determine Physical Locations
ttps.procedure_description: ASA searches for physical-location information on Israeli military bases and the Israeli Air Force flight academy, using mapping resources such as Wikimapia[.]org and correlating Instagram geolocation with OpenStreetMap.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim geolocation reconnaissance; not detectable in defender telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Gather Victim Network Information: Domain Properties
ttps.procedure_description: ASA uses subdomainfinder.c99[.]nl to enumerate subdomains and domain properties of target organizations during reconnaissance.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — passive subdomain enumeration via third-party services is off-victim; hunt via attack-surface monitoring of your own exposed subdomains

ttps.procedure_description: ASA uses the Masscan application to scan IP blocks, including enumerating internet-facing hosts running Real Time Streaming Protocol on TCP/554 across Israel, Gaza and Iran to locate accessible IP cameras.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — mass port scanning (esp. RTSP/554 sweeps) against internet-facing assets is observable via perimeter/IDS, netflow and honeypot telemetry, though source IPs are VPN-fronted and attribution is hard

ttps.procedure_description: ASA runs vulnerability scans against target infrastructure using Acunetix and Burp Suite to identify exploitable web-application flaws prior to exploitation.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — web-app vulnerability scanning generates distinctive request patterns detectable via WAF/IDS and web-server log analysis

ttps.procedure_description: ASA acquires access to previously-leaked datasets containing account credentials from online resources such as ghostproject[.]fr, reusing them against targets and to enrich victim profiling.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — acquisition of leaked data is off-victim; the downstream credential reuse is where detection becomes feasible (authentication anomaly monitoring)

ttps.procedure_description: ASA acquires operational infrastructure through commercial VPN providers (Private Internet Access, Windscribe, ExpressVPN, Urban VPN, NordVPN) for anonymization, and procures operational servers via its own fictitious cover-hosting resellers 'Server-Speed' (server-speed[.]com) and 'VPS-Agent' (vps-agent[.]net), themselves upstreamed from BAcloud (Lithuania) and Stark Industries/PQ Hosting (UK/Moldova).
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — infrastructure acquisition is off-victim; a HUNT/attribution surface via reseller pivots and VPN-node reputation, and the advisory notes VPN nodes are shared so are not exclusive indicators

ttps.procedure_description: ASA registers persona and operational domains for influence and hosting operations, including cybercourt[.]io, zeusistalking[.]io/net/com, rgud-group[.]net/com, pro-today[.]org, onlinelive[.]info, cyberflood[.]io, Contact-hstg[.]com and il-cert[.]net (used for RAT C2).
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — domain registration is off-victim; a HUNT signal via newly-registered/lookalike-domain feeds and persona-domain clustering

ttps.procedure_description: ASA stands up and abuses web/cloud services — including its own cover-hosting reseller storefronts (VPS-Agent, Server-Speed) and generative-AI SaaS (Remini, Voicemod, Murf AI, Appy Pie) — to provision servers and produce influence content while providing plausible deniability that malicious infrastructure came from a legitimate provider.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim service acquisition; a hunt/attribution artifact rather than a host or log detection

ttps.procedure_description: A hallmark of the actor: creating fictitious cover personas and sock-puppet/cover-hacktivist social-media presences — 'Cyber Court' (Telegram @cybercourt_io), 'Cyber Flood', 'For-Humanity', 'Regiment GUD', 'Zeus is Talking', 'Anzu Team', 'Makhlab al-Nasr', 'NET Hunter', 'Emirate Students Movement' — to amplify influence messaging and manufacture apparent grassroots hacktivism.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — persona creation is entirely off-victim; a HUNT/attribution artifact (persona-network mapping, avatar/handle reuse, cross-platform linkage), not a host or log detection

ttps.procedure_description: ASA establishes email/messaging accounts under fabricated personas to send intimidation messages (e.g. Contact-HSTG SMS to hostage families) and to operate its cover-hosting reseller businesses (e.g. Info@Vps-Agent[.]Net).
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — account creation is off-victim; only the inbound intimidation messages themselves are observable, on the recipient side

ttps.procedure_description: ASA weaponized an exploit for CVE-2023-38831 (WinRAR) for use in its operations, per the advisory's Resource Development mapping.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — exploit development is off-victim; downstream exploitation attempts are the detection surface

ttps.procedure_description: ASA obtains and operates commercially/openly available tooling — Masscan, Acunetix, Burp Suite and SQLMap for scanning and exploitation, and hash-cracking and OSINT services — living off widely-available tools to reduce custom-malware exposure.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — the tools are legitimate, but their on-target use (SQLMap injection strings, Acunetix/Burp scan signatures) is detectable via WAF/IDS and web-log analytics

ttps.procedure_description: ASA stages its WezRat payload on actor-controlled web infrastructure (onlinelive[.]info, with C2 fetch/report paths /wez/insert.php and /wez/api.php) so the trojanized 'Google Chrome Installer.msi' can retrieve and beacon to it post-execution.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — staging on attacker infrastructure is off-victim; the resulting client callbacks (T1071.001) are the detection surface

ttps.procedure_description: ASA exploits internet-facing applications and content-management systems to gain access, notably using SQLMap for SQL-injection against target infrastructure, and seeking mass-compromise opportunities against shared hosting providers or a common CMS used by a sector. Public-facing exploitation also underpinned access to the compromised French dynamic-display provider and IPTV/streaming services.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — SQL-injection and web-exploitation attempts are detectable via WAF/IPS signatures, anomalous web-server child-process spawns, and web-application logging; this is a primary DETECTION surface for the actor

ttps.procedure_description: ASA leverages unauthorized/valid access to third-party services for influence delivery — e.g. accessing a US IPTV streaming service to inject 'For-Humanity' messaging, accessing internet-facing IP-camera streams, and accessing the compromised French dynamic-display provider to push montages.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — anomalous logins to streaming/display/admin panels from VPN ASNs and impossible-travel analytics can surface valid-account abuse, though it can resemble legitimate use

ttps.procedure_description: ASA induces victims to run a trojanized 'Google Chrome Installer.msi' that masquerades as a legitimate Chrome security-patch installer; the altered MSI installs Chrome but then executes the embedded, heavily-obfuscated 'bd.exe' (WezRat) RAT.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — msiexec spawning an unexpected child executable (bd.exe) and MSI package integrity/signing anomalies are detectable via process-creation and EDR telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: ASA accesses victim infrastructure via automated password-guessing attempts against exposed accounts and services.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — repeated authentication failures across accounts/services are detectable via authentication-log analytics and lockout monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: ASA cracks obtained password hashes offline using online resources such as crackstation[.]net, hashes[.]com and md5hashing[.]net.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — offline hash cracking occurs entirely on attacker/third-party resources with no victim-side telemetry; a hunt/awareness item

ttps.procedure_description: The WezRat 'bd.exe' RAT is heavily obfuscated and requires a runtime de-obfuscation key passed on the command line (observed value '8765') to decode its embedded configuration, including the C2 web-server address, impeding static analysis.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — obfuscation defeats static signatures; hunt via entropy analysis, the published WezRat detection content, and behavioral (decode-then-beacon) analytics

ttps.technique_name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
ttps.procedure_description: ASA disguises malicious artifacts and personas as legitimate: the RAT dropper is named 'Google Chrome Installer.msi' and performs a real Chrome install to appear benign; the C2 domain il-cert[.]net (connect.il-cert[.]net) mimics a security/CERT resource; and the 'Regiment GUD' persona impersonates the real French far-right group 'GUD'.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — name/location masquerade defeats name-based trust; a HUNT via signer/metadata mismatch, MSI-behavior anomaly and lookalike-domain analysis

ttps.procedure_description: The WezRat RAT beacons over HTTP web protocols to its C2, checking in for tasking and returning collected data — observed communicating to http://onlinelive[.]info/wez/insert.php and http://onlinelive[.]info/wez/api.php (and C2 host connect.il-cert[.]net), with the C2 host address decoded from the obfuscated config at runtime. It can persist by being added to the Windows Startup directory.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — HTTP beaconing to the known WezRat C2 paths/domains and periodic web callbacks are detectable via network/proxy logging, DNS monitoring and IOC matching

ttps.procedure_description: The trojanized MSI retrieves and executes the WezRat payload, and the RAT can pull additional instructions/content from its C2 web server — transferring tooling into the victim environment after initial execution.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — post-install downloads of executable content and new-binary drops correlated with process lineage are detectable via EDR and proxy telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: ASA deploys the WezRat remote access trojan (mapped to T1219 in the advisory's C2 table) which collects basic system information, checks in to a specified web server when run from the command line, and awaits interactive tasking — providing hands-off-keyboard remote control of infected hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — RAT beaconing, command-line-launched implant behavior and the known WezRat hashes/C2 give a workable detection surface via EDR and network IOCs

ttps.procedure_description: Upon execution, the WezRat RAT collects basic system information about the infected computer to report to its C2, per the advisory's description of the 'bd' program's behavior.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — host-enumeration API/command patterns from a freshly-spawned implant are detectable via EDR behavioral analytics, though individually low-signal

ttps.procedure_description: Central to the actor's hack-and-leak model: after stealing data ASA exfiltrates and publishes it (and harvested IP-camera content) via actor-controlled web services and servers, making stolen material available to 'clients' and leaking it to inflict reputational/psychological damage.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — exfiltration to web services can blend with normal outbound web traffic; hunt via large/anomalous outbound transfers to newly-seen destinations and DLP, though the leak itself often surfaces externally first

ttps.procedure_description: As part of its cyber-enabled influence operations, ASA defaces and hijacks externally-visible surfaces to display crafted propaganda — e.g. injecting Israel-Hamas-war messaging into a compromised US IPTV stream ('For-Humanity'), pushing anti-Israel photo montages via a compromised French dynamic-display provider during the 2024 Olympics, and website defacements against Israeli targets.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — external defacement/content-injection is detectable via file-integrity monitoring, 'known-good' content baselining and external brand/surface monitoring; a DETECTION surface for the influence payoff

detection_signals: Inbound mass port scanning against internet-facing assets, especially RTSP TCP/554 sweeps (Masscan) — correlate source IPs against the advisory's VPN-fronted IP list before action
Web-application logs showing SQL-injection / SQLMap and Acunetix/Burp scanner signatures against public-facing apps and CMS
msiexec.exe spawning an unexpected child process (bd.exe) shortly after a 'Google Chrome Installer.msi' execution; MSI signature/integrity anomalies
Command line containing a bare numeric de-obfuscation argument (e.g. '8765') passed to an unsigned executable
HTTP callbacks to onlinelive[.]info/wez/insert.php or /wez/api.php, or to C2 host connect.il-cert[.]net

File hash matches for WezRat: SHA256 4431b2a4d7758907f81fb1a0c1e36b2ce03e08d43123b1c398487770afd20727 (First.exe) and 6f765dda126e830c6cd2c7938dbb970d03be728e82c00388903a4ef3f9ecc853 (Google Chrome Installer.msi)
New executable added to the Windows Startup directory correlated with recent web-beaconing (WezRat persistence)
Successful authentications originating from Private Internet Access / Windscribe / ExpressVPN / Urban VPN / NordVPN exit nodes to sensitive/admin services
File-integrity / content-baseline alerts on externally-served content (websites, digital-signage, streaming feeds) indicating defacement or content injection
Outbound connections to actor persona/leak/staging domains (cybercourt[.]io, zeusistalking[.]*, rgud-group[.]*, cyberflood[.]io, pro-today[.]org, Contact-hstg[.]com)
notes: GROUP-ID DISCREPANCY (important for downstream): the task brief states MITRE tracks Emennet Pasargad as G1009 and to use it as the base mapping, but in THIS environment's bundled/reorganized ATT&CK dataset G1009 = 'Moses Staff' (DEV-0500 / Marigold Sandstorm) and G1044 = 'APT42' — neither is Emennet Pasargad / Cotton Sandstorm, and no dedicated Emennet Pasargad group object exists in this dataset. actor.mitre_id and actor.mitre_canonical_name are therefore left empty rather than asserting an unverifiable/incorrect ID; Moses Staff is listed under related_clusters solely to flag the collision, NOT as an alias. All 32 ttps were built from the actor's OWN ATT&CK table in advisory AA24-233A (v15.1) plus Microsoft-sourced enrichment, and EVERY technique_id was verified present in this dataset via sigma.data.mitre_attack; T1656 (Impersonation) was evaluated but is NOT in this dataset and was dropped (the Regiment-GUD/GUD and il-cert masquerade behavior is instead carried under T1036.005). SOURCE-HYGIENE: the brief's cited 'AA24-290A' is a DIFFERENT advisory ('Iranian Cyber Actors' Brute Force and Credential Access Activity', Zerologon/CVE-2020-1472, unrelated brute-force actor); its IPs/SHA1 hashes/CVE were deliberately EXCLUDED to avoid poisoning the pack — the correct Emennet Pasargad advisory is AA24-233A / IC3 241030 / JCSA-20241030-001. IOC caveats from the advisory itself: listed IPs are largely shared commercial-VPN exit nodes (Private Internet Access etc.), are not exclusive to the actor, and should be used for retrospective hunting, not blind blocking; two 85.206.x entries are CIDR-style ranges preserved verbatim. Tactic slugs use this dataset's conventions (defense-evasion emitted as 'stealth'). No YARA rules were present verbatim in the fetched primary sources, so yara_rules is empty (none authored). This actor is influence/hack-and-leak-centric, so much of the kill chain (personas, cover-hosting, leak-site operations, OSINT) is inherently HUNT (low feasibility, off-victim); the concrete DETECTION surfaces are T1190 public-app/CMS exploitation, T1595.* mass/RTSP scanning, the trojanized-MSI→WezRat execution & HTTP C2 chain, and T1491.002 external defacement/content-injection of served surfaces.
